paragraphs.text: For much of the past 70,000 years, the Sahara in North Africa has closely resembled the desert it is today. Some 12,000 years ago, however, a wobble in the Earth's axis and other factors caused Africa's seasonal monsoon rains to shift slightly north. Lush watersheds began to stretch across the Sahara bringing animal life and eventually people. Archaeologists have made inventories of the patterns inscribed on the ceramics of these early inhabitants of the Green Sahara. They have also identified thousands of their rock engravings, which depict herds of ostriches, giraffes, and elephants. Some of the images suggest that the people of the Green Sahara learned to domesticate cattle. But they remain veiled in mystery. Archaeologists are uncertain whether these people arrived there from the Mediterranean coast, central African jungles, or the Nile Valley, and whether they were nomads, or staked out territories and built permanent homes there. It is also unclear how, when the monsoons receded, the people coped with a drying landscape.

Seeking answers to such questions is normally the domain of anthropologists and archaeologists, but the palaeontologist Paul Sereno of the University of Chicago also became involved. Sereno's field was the study of prehistoric life, but while he was on an expedition tracing down dinosaur remains in the Ténéré desert in the south of the Sahara, he stumbled across human remains. He decided to contact Elena Garcea, an archaeologist at the University of Cassino, in Italy, and invite her to accompany him to the site where he had discovered the human remains. Garcea had spent three decades working digs along the Nile in Sudan and in the mountains of the Libyan Desert, and was well acquainted with the ancient peoples of the Sahara.

When they arrived at the site, which they called Gobero, they found dozens of human skeletons in various degrees of completeness, far more than Garcea had seen at all her other digs combined. They also discovered small pieces of clay pots. The markings on some were identified as belonging to a people known to scholars as the Tenerian, a nomadic herding culture that thrived during the later part of the Green Sahara era, 6,500 to 4,500 years ago. Other pots were identified as Kiffian. The Kiffian were a fishing-based culture and lived during the early wet period, between 10,000 and 8,000 years ago.

Over the next three weeks, Sereno and Garcea, along with a team of excavators, walked carefully around the site and drew a map. They exhumed eight burials and collected artefacts from both cultures. As the team worked, it became apparent that there were stark differences in the burials. Some appeared to be little more than a tight bundle of bones, as if the body had been bound or squeezed into a basket, which had long since decomposed. Carbon particulars believed that the most of these individuals were surprisingly large — as much as six feet eight inches tall — and thick bones, by contrast, other skeletons belonged to much smaller people, about five-and-a-half feet tall. But until the age of the bones could be determined, no one could say for sure which were Kiffian and which were Tenerian.

Sereno carefully took out some teeth, one from each of four skulls, and sent them to a lab for radiocarbon dating. The results suggested the tightly bundled burials were 8,000 years old, the heart of the Kiffian era, while the smaller skeletons turned out to be about 6,000 years old, well within the Tenerian period. At least now the scientists knew who was who.

The bundles of Kiffian bones came with few artefacts to shed light on their culture. But bones alone can say a lot about the daily lives of a vanished people. Even at the site, Arizona State University bio-archaeologist Chris Stojanowski could begin to piece together some clues. Judging by the bones, the Kiffian appeared to be a peaceful, hardworking people. 'The lack of injuries suggests they weren't doing much fighting,' he said. 'And these guys were strong.' He pointed to a long, narrow ridge running along a femur. 'That's his muscle attachment,' he said. 'It's huge, which meant he had a rather strenuous life, and it also shows he ate a lot of protein — something else that's consistent with a fishing way of life.' For contrast, he showed me the femur of a Tenerian male. The ridge was barely perceptible. 'This guy had a more sedentary lifestyle,' he said, 'which you'd expect of a herder.'

Unlike their predecessors, the Tenerian often adorned their graves with artefacts, including tools crafted from a green volcanic rock, quarried about a hundred miles away in the Air mountains. Stojanowski's assessment that they were herders fits the prevailing view among scholars. But if the Tenerian were herders, Sereno pointed out, where were the herds? Among the hundreds of animal bones that had turned up at the site, none belonged to goats or sheep, and only three came from a cow. 'It's not unusual for a herding culture not to slaughter their animals, particularly in a cemetery,' Garcea explained, adding that even modern pastoralists, such as Niger's Wodaabe, are loath to butcher even one animal in their herd. It would seem, Sereno reasoned, the Tenerian at Gobero were experiencing a transition. They had not fully adopted herding and still relied heavily on hunting for their survival.

The twilight of the Green Sahara might have been the perfect time to be living at Gobero. But the Green Sahara's climate was rapidly changing and the abundance of food was short-lived. Before long, the Tenerian were gone, leaving only bones and a few artefacts to bear witness to their existence.
